editorials.title: Service quality in focus as telecos ring in hikes
editorials.passage: Telecom tariffs in India are back in spotlight with analysts expecting a broad-based increase in the coming months after a two-year pause. Recent stealth price hikes by the country’s two leading telecom operators have fuelled anticipation of a 10-15 percent industry-wide increase. If Bharti Airtel removed its select entry-level prepaid plans with 28-to-60-day validity, effectively raising the price of some of its lower-end offerings earlier this month, Reliance Jio followed suit with a similar move. While it retained its entry-level data plan intact, it reintroduced Jio Prime membership at a one-time fee of ₹300. This price protection guarantee till September 2027, in a way, signals that a hike is likely in the next six months, according to brokerage Motilal Oswal Financial Services. Another factor prompting speculation over higher tariffs is that price hikes in India often follow a 2-3 year cycle and the last such increase occurred in July 2024.Raised rates in the past have led to higher average per-user revenues of about ₹15-20 a month even though operators lose subscribers. Data from the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India shows that the three leading operators—Jio, Airtel and Vodafone—together shed 23.14 million subscribers between June and September of 2024 following the last round of hikes. Indian customers are now moving away from being price-sensitive to value-sensitive decisions, while operators are shifting focus from infrastructure rollouts to revenue generation. This is essential given that India is the world’s second-largest telecom market by subscriber base. Of the total 1.348 billion connections, the broadband subscriber base alone surged past 1.08 billion owing to rising smartphone use, affordable tariffs and growing demand for high-speed connectivity in both urban and rural areas..Even though teledensity stood at over 90 percent, expanding connectivity and improving service quality in rural and remote areas remain a challenge. Call drops continue to be a major problem, with operators facing intense pressure to improve network reliability and deliver uninterrupted data services. At the same time, adoption of next-generation technologies such as internet-of-things and Cloud-based communications has increased cybersecurity risks. All of this means telecom companies must strengthen network security and safeguard customer data at all costs. editorials.title: More needed than pact to address social media addiction among kids
editorials.passage: In a landmark deal with potentially far-reaching beneficial impact on children, Meta Platforms on Wednesday agreed to pay up to $18 billion over the next 10 years and strictly limit how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram. The agreement with almost all US states followed a trial over allegations that Meta’s products were harmful as its social media platforms are designed to get children addicted. The agreement, which cut short multiple lawsuits, requires Meta to disable most push-notifications to teenagers during school hours and enhance measures to prevent them from accessing age-restricted content. It is hoped that such limits can be tightened further if other social media platforms like YouTube and Snapchat adopt similar terms to help tackle growing social media addiction among youngsters.The accord is being seen as an unprecedented template to resolve thousands of other lawsuits against social media companies. Not just the US, governments across the world are trying to grapple with the issue. Australia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Brazil have banned or mandated strict parental control for social media use by children under 16; the UK is considering a similar move. Several Indian states are talking along the same line..Social media addiction is known to cause a range of problems among the young, particularly mental health issues (depression and anxiety, low self-esteem, sleep disruption); brain and cognitive effects (shortened attention span and reduced grey matter, particularly affecting parts of the brain linked to self-control and decision-making); withdrawal symptoms when staying offline (social isolation, lower productivity and strain in relationships)—all contributing to mental health issues. Many of these have ended tragically in suicides in India and elsewhere—which is why the Wednesday accord is viewed as a much-welcome development.However, addressing these problems requires much more than what the deal promises. Experts—including influential social and cultural psychologist Jonathan Haidt—have pointed out that Meta’s still-running AI-powered recommendation engine continues to maximise engagement with harmful content. This brings into play the importance of responsible parenting, robust counselling (in academic institutions and outside) and governmental controls that pay close attention to the cultural contexts of countries and communities. The social, mental and neurological well-being of children is at stake. editorials.title: Quick Take | For cooler homes
editorials.passage: As Italy faces the summer’s most intense heatwave this weekend, fresh number-crunching by a Spanish health research institute reveals 35,000 more deaths than usual during Europe’s four record-breaking heatwaves this year. Excess mortality in Germany, France and Spain alone crossed 25,000, according to the provisional estimate. Other numbers from the International Energy Agency set the context: only one in four European households had air-conditioning in 2025, compared to nine out of 10 in Japan and the US; the comparable number for India is closer to one in 20. While this is music to the ears of AC salespeople, the longer-term planning for all countries must involve serious rethinking of how we build houses. editorials.title: Shared warts
editorials.passage:
We are in the midst of something like a democratic spring in the country. By this, we mean the dramatic return of the ‘spirit’ of democracy even as its institutional flesh and bones remain in a morbid rot.

The spirit of democracy, as the philosopher, Cornelius Castoriadis, described it, inheres in the radical questioning of the prevailing institutional order through which society is organised. We have seen sporadic outbursts of this democratic spirit quite a few times over the last decade. It has animated the protest movements of farmers and factory workers as well as those by tribals, Muslims and Dalits over State-backed attempts to marginalise them in the institutional power structure. The youth prot­ests, spreading out from Jantar Mantar into a decentralised movement of schoolchildren demanding basic facilities in public schools, have perhaps been the most striking manifestation of this democratic spirit. The protests managed to activate a grassroots Gen Z/teenage constituency long considered politically inert and also mobilised a cross-cutting social coalition in opposition to an unfair system of education.

Can this democratic spring lead to the restoration of the health of our democratic institutions? How serious is the challenge posed by the youth movement to the still dominant Hindu nationalist order of the Bharatiya Janata Party?

Both questions hinge on the capacity of Opposition parties to channel this democratic spirit into an alternative ‘social imaginary’. The dominant social imaginary — the framework through which the State understands and organises society — offers little space for the educational and employment aspirations of a restless youth constituency. The question, then, is whether the Opposition can offer such an alternative social imaginary which is built around the aspirations of our young men and women.

But first, we need to understand why the BJP has been so successful in winning and then holding on to power in 21st-century India. Even during the years of UPA rule, the BJP managed to consolidate a stable political order in states such as Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. The last time an incumbent Congress-­led government won re-election in a state was in Arunachal Pradesh in 2014. Since then, no Congress-led state government has secured a successive term, although an incumbent coalition in which the Congress was a junior partner retained Jharkhand in 2024. The BJP’s establishment as the ‘natural ruling party’ of India is not just due to the popular attraction of its Hindu nationalist ideology. It also owes much to the symbiotic relationship between its ideological framework and the social imaginary of the contemporary neoliberal State.

A social imaginary can be thought of as something like the master software for the State which directs the functioning of its bureaucratic institutions. It is a symbolic framework of ideas and values through which State institutions recognise and represent the social world via categories of demarcation and, then, organise the various forces of society towards building a specific social and political order. The BJP in power runs the State through a compound social imaginary — what we shall call neoliberal Hindutva , a powerful and complementary mode of representing and organising social forces. We miss the significance of this mutually reinforcing fusion of Hindu nationalist world view with the neoliberal institutional order when we treat Hindutva and neoliberalism as two separate ideologies that happen to coexist.

Of the two legs of the social imaginary, Hindutva bears the load of representing the social world — who belongs, who threatens, what constitutes the core political subject that represents the demos . The neoliberal leg bears the bulk of the load for supplying the techniques of organising society — targeted welfare, State-business compact, shrunken and segmented public institutions. Neoliberal governance strengthens the representational claim of Hindu identity as the primary political category by acting as a powerful solvent on the institutional basis of class and caste politics.

In the Narendra Modi era, a key shift in welfare delivery — the expansion of cash transfer schemes — has depoliticised welfare by bypassing collective mobilisation and reducing workers to individual beneficiaries rather than organised claim-makers. At the same time, the contracting and the outsourcing of employment to informal production centres has undermined the significance of the workplace as a site of collective mobilisation of workers. Neoliberalism has also weakened the institutional basis of caste politics through the shrinkage of the public sector. The steady march of privatisation, disinvestment and outsourcing has not only reduced the scope of caste-based affirmative action but also eroded an important political base for the organisation of collective action and the distribution of patronage. At the other end of the bargain, Hindutva reinforces the popular acceptance of neoliberal techniques of governance.

As a standalone social imaginary, neoliberalism is inherently unstable, particularly in a society like India where winners and losers of neoliber­alism stack up along the lines of caste hierarchy. There is an ever-present dan­ger of a volatile political articulation of distributive conflicts ge­n­erated by the reorganisation of land, labour, knowledge and natural resources.

What Hindutva does is provide a popular justification for concentrating executive power in the name of fighting the (Muslim-coded) threats of infiltration, jihad , demographic imbalance. This executive power is then deployed in the coercive reorganisation of society. Simultaneously, Hindutva offers a facsimile of popular participation in the re-institution of society into a Hindu nation. Of course, the attraction of the claim of inclusion based on a privileged Hindu identity is derived in large part from the exclusion of minorities in citizenship entitlements like voting rights, housing, welfare, and civic amenities.

In contrast, Opposition parties have struggled to translate their stated ideologies into a coherent social imaginary for organising socio-economic life. This is particularly true of the Congress whose ideological claims bear little resemblance to its governance in states like Telangana and Karnataka which relies on the same techniques of coercive neoliberalism as those of the BJP.

Under Rahul Gandhi, the Cong­ress has taken to portraying the main dividing line of society as between the bottom 90% (marginalised castes and non-elite classes) excluded from institutional power and the oligarchs that control institutional power.

Yet in Karnataka, the Congress under D.K. Shivakumar runs the archetype of the neoliberal “land-broker” State where the State facilitates big corporations in the acquisition of land in rural and peri-urban areas. One can find no better example of the regime of “dispossession without development”, as the anthropologist, Michael Levien, characterised it than Shivakumar’s pet project, Greater Bengaluru Integrated Township. Using its power of eminent domain, the government has acquired thousands of acres of village lands, converting them into speculative real estate commodities for property developers and large corporate houses. The same logic pervades the proposed transportation corridor running through Bengaluru, which a dissenting citizen group has called “vanity infrastructure” and a “real estate project in disguise”. In the design of the project, the convenience of the city’s people appears far less important than enabling lucrative profits for big private players, with Gautam Adani presumed to be the lead contractor-cum-concessionaire. In particular, the restriction of the tunnel to car owners — roughly 3% of the city’s population — and the exclusion of two-wheelers and auto-rickshaws have been criticised as a marker of ‘economic apartheid’.

Or consider the Telangana government’s reliance on the all-powerful ‘anti-encroachment’ enforcement agency called HYDRAA, set up to demolish structures deemed to be unauthorised. In fact, the chief minister, Revanth Reddy, saw fit to claim (mistakenly) that the agency’s name had been inspired by a similar initiative of Hitler, a revealing glimpse of the disciplinary logic of authoritarian neoliberalism that informs governance in that Congress-ruled state.

The issues animating the youth protests — jobless growth and a dila­pidated public education system —are longstanding problems inherited by the Modi government rather than created by it. The moment calls for an Opposition capable of providing substantive solutions to the travails of India’s young. This requires a fresh imagination of how our social and economic life should be organised and to what end. This needs a break with the neoliberal consensus that brought us here. Yet we still don’t find a credible offering of an alternative social imaginary on the political menu.

Asim Ali is a political researcher and columnist

editorials.title: When rail takes wing
editorials.passage:
Some months ago, the railways minister, Ashwini Vaishnaw, had advised airline sector investors to “please take note”, warning that India’s upcoming high-speed rail network would dominate the key short-haul routes. The railways minister’s view deserves serious attention.

High-speed railway corridors were not promised in an election rally. The Union budget of 2026-27 had announced seven high-speed rail corridors spanning nearly 4,000 kilometres, with an estimated overlay cost of Rs 16 lakh crore. India’s first bullet train is also set to launch in August 2027 on the Mumbai-Ahmedabad corridor using E5 Japanese Shinkansen technology. The travel time proposed for the project is equally striking: Mumbai to Pune would take 48 minutes; Bengaluru to Chennai can be covered in 78 minutes; Hyderabad to Bengaluru would take 2 hours and 8 minutes. These are not train timings; they are flight timings — minus the airport!

To understand why the railways minister’s remark matters, one must first appreciate what Indian aviation has become. For the majority of the last decade, India was the world’s fastest-growing major aviation market, a distinction that attracted aircraft manufacturers, global carriers, and capital alike. In 2023, Air India placed the largest aircraft purchase order in aviation history — for the purchase of 470 aircraft from Airbus and Boeing. In a matter of a few months, this record was broken by Indigo, which placed an order of 500 Airbus jets at the Paris Air Show, taking its backlog towards 1,000 aircraft. The government has projected over 350 airports by 2047, with passenger traffic eventually crossing the one-billion mark. International carriers from Turkey to Hungary were queuing to enter this market. For a decade, Indian aviation was not merely growing — it was widely regarded as one of the defining economic stories of the era.

But the aviation sector is already revealing structural strain that its headline numbers conceal. India’s airlines carried over 165 million passengers in FY2025 — a 7.6% year-on-year increase — and subsequently incurred nearly Rs 5,289.73 crore in losses. Growth was no longer a problem; profitability was. Between July and September 2025, domestic passenger numbers fell year on year, the first such sustained decline since the Covid-19 pandemic. In April 2026, traffic dropped 4.2% from the previous month, with the figures also trailing those of April 2025. India’s aviation ambitions, it turns out, have long been sustained on margins that were too thin to absorb international disruptions.

The international evidence offers little comfort to those dismissing the challenge to airlines from railways. Research examining aviation response to high-speed railways entry across major economies like Japan, South Korea and China has found consistent and material reductions in airline seat capacity on competing routes. Competition tends to be the fiercest where the railway can deliver city-centred journeys within roughly two to three hours — precisely the window that the proposed Indian corridors target. For instance, in Europe, the arrival of high-speed rail between Frankfurt and Cologne caused air passenger numbers to collapse by two-thirds within three years: the route was then permanently withdrawn in 2009. Korean research estimated demand reductions of 34% to 75% on air routes where the Korea Train Express competed directly. In China, airlines faced billion-dollar domestic losses and pivoted towards international routes in response. The Tokyo-Osaka Shinkansen corridor is where this logic reaches its conclusion: rail holds a 99% share.

What is being constructed along India’s high-speed rail corridors is more than fast trains. It is a reorganisation of economic geography. KPMG’s analysis of the budget of 2026 noted that the corridors are expected to create secondary economic nodes, reduce pressure on congested metros, and catalyse transit-oriented industrial clusters along the routes. The railways ministry has described connected cities as “integrated economic zones”. When Ahmedabad and Mumbai are under two hours apart, with Surat, Baroda, and Vapi (major economic cities) in between, they stop functioning as separate units and begin operating as a single economic belt.

These seven corridors are deliberately distributed. The western network links Ahmedabad, Mumbai, and Pune. The southern triangle connects Hyderabad, Bengaluru, and Chennai. The northern axis runs from Delhi through Varanasi to Siliguri, the gateway to India’s Northeast. These areas are described in the budget documents as “growth connectors”. These corridors also amount to a national spatial strategy, not merely a regional infrastructure project.

Of course, none of this is guaranteed. The Mumbai-Ahmedabad corridor was groundbreaking back in 2017, targeted for 2023-24, and now anticipates a partial opening between Surat and Bilimora in August 2027. Land acquisition — as admitted by the railways minister — has been the biggest bottleneck in India’s ambitious infrastructure push. Ticket pricing will decide whether the middle-income traveller chooses speed over savings: India’s pricing history on rail has not always prioritised accessibility. Moreover, the airlines are not passive actors: they are already redirecting capacity toward international routes — Mumbai-Dubai, Delhi-London, that no rail corridor can reach. Aviation will adapt. It will not simply disappear.

The minister may be directionally correct and chronologically optimistic. High-speed rail, on accumulated global evidence, will come to dominate the 300-800 km corridors where it competes directly with airlines. But the shift will take years rather than months, and its success will depend on an execution record that India’s infrastructure history demands we scrutinise, not assume.

What India is entering is a modal re-ordering. Trains will reclaim short and medium corridors where they can genuinely compete. Airlines will be pushed towards longer hauls and international markets wherein no platform announcement can reach them. The domestic golden age of Indian aviation may be entering its final chapter. The relevant question for investors and policymakers is not whether the train arrives. It is whether they have already moved to a different terminal.

Shweta Mohan is Assistant Professor of Economics and Avinash Verma research assistant and student at National University of Study and Research in Law, Ranchi

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: Getting a sanitary pad in offices and colleges is a high-tech obstacle
editorials.passage:
Sir — Nothing kills the mood quite like discovering that your period has arrived, only to encounter a high-tech obstacle in the washroom. Getting a sanitary pad often requires navigating a complicated dispenser in many offices and colleges. While a woman stands in a bathroom hoping not to stain her clothes, the machine demands a QR code scan, an OTP, and ID proof. It is the equivalent of bleeding from a cut arm while having to complete a two-factor authentication process just for a bandage. This setup feels suspiciously like the work of someone who has never experienced a period emergency.

Sir — The flash floods in Nepal and Tibet have taken the lives of at least 469 people while more than 1,400 are missing (“Nepal flash flood catastrophe”, Aug 27). The deluge swept away people, animals and goods as well as critical infrastructure, including power plants. More than a hundred Indian devotees, most of whom had travelled to the region on pilgrimage to Kailash Mansarovar, remain unaccounted for.

Sir — A glacial collapse led to the flash floods in Nepal and Tibet (“Washed away”, Aug 28). With extreme weather events, including flash floods and cloudbursts, occurring with alarming frequency, concerted measures to improve the accuracy of warning systems have assumed greater significance than ever. The timely evacuation of people from disaster-hit zones needs to be more robust.

M. Jeyaram, Sholavandan, Tamil Nadu

Sir — The Nepal-Tibet flash floods appear to have resulted from a high mountain ice-and-rock burst which was followed by debris flow that swept through central Nepal. India, particularly the Himalayan states and the flood-prone plains downstream, must treat this as a serious warning. Authorities should strengthen early-warning systems and improve drainage and embankments.

Sir — The flash flood from the Bhote Koshi river in Nepal, which has claimed many lives and devastated infrastructure and properties worth millions, may have been exacerbated by the failure of alert and response systems. Governments must learn from these repeated warnings and work to improve the environment.

Manzar Imam Qasmi, Purnea, Bihar

Sir — Rescuers are racing to locate people missing near the severely affected areas after a massive wall of water crashed down following a catastrophic glacial collapse in Nepal on Wednesday. Despite the Himalayan belt’s vulnerability to such disasters, countries continue to push infrastructure projects in the region.

Sir — The flood catastrophe in Nepal is not simply a natural calamity; it is also a man-made crisis driven by climate change. Rising temperatures melt glaciers and trigger extreme weather events that do not respect national borders. Asian countries cannot afford to wait for global consensus while local communities drown.

Sir — The visuals of devastation emerging from Nepal are heartbreaking. It is true that nature’s fury cannot be averted. But the glacial collapse, which is suspected to have been caused by the melting of the permafrost, is not just nature’s fury. It is the result of climate change. Such events will thus become more frequent.

As Nepal’s minister for foreign affairs has correctly pointed out, there should be cooperation among India, Nepal, China and Bhutan when it comes to dealing with the ecology of the Himalayan region.

D.V.G. Sankara Rao, Andhra Pradesh

editorials.title: Let the mind bloom: Editorial on NITI Aayog report’s red flags for India’s research and development
editorials.passage:
NITI Aayog’s report, Ease of Doing Research & Development in India , has underlined a number of red flags that afflict research and development in this country. One of the challenges concerns funding. India spends about 0.65% of its GDP on R&D, compared to 2.4% in China, 3.5% in the United States of America and 4.5% in South Korea. It recommends that India reach at least 2% within four to five years. That target requires higher public spending and stronger incentives for private research. Grant decisions should be completed within six months. Funding agencies need professional project-management teams. State science councils require more resources and state universities must fill regular faculty posts. Additionally, review panels must draw members in a representative manner.

But funding volume is not the only problem. More than 80% of funding from the Anusandhan National Re­search Foundation, the apex statutory body meant to provide direction in this field, reportedly goes to the Indian Institutes of Technology even as state universities struggle with inadequate laboratories, vacant posts, and poor administrative support. Researchers also face delayed disbursal of fellowships, slow procurement and repeated paperwork. The concentration of grants within a small coterie of elite institutions has consequences. State universities are the preferred choice of students hailing from poorer, rural and marginalised communities. Meagre investments in these institutions restrict their access to careers in pure research and perpetuate privilege.

Another impediment highlighted by the NITI Aayog report is that of opacity. In response, it has proposed a Unified Architecture for Project Management System mandatory for State-funded research. Each grant should receive a permanent identification number, stating who received the money, how it was spent and what the project produced. It should also disclose the selection process, peer-review standards, project milestones, independent evaluations and any retractions. Papers and patents alone cannot establish quality. The system must show whether findings of the research withstand scrutiny and whether public money produced credible knowledge. Failed experiments should be recorded without penalising honest scientific work. Such a culture of transparency would help identify unproductive investments and stop the duplication of precious grants. A unified database could also resist ideological and political interference. Despite denials from the government, there have been persistent whispers of restrictions being posed on the choice of subject for researchers. The NITI Aayog’s UPMS could be useful in informing the public whether research funds are being used to address crucial issues such as health, agriculture, clean energy or being disbursed to politically-favoured institutions pursuing ideological agenda of doubtful scientific value. Similarly, withdrawal of funds from research must carry published reasons. An environment conducive to free thinking is a must if research is to bear fruit.

It would be myopic to limit the potential of India’s R&D sector to social and economic growth. The attendant gains of a robust R&D framework include, among other things, encouragement for intellectual curiosity, debates and questioning and the kindling of the scientific spirit. Each of these elements is necessary to deepen democracy’s roots. A stilted research culture is thus inimical to the cause of Indian democracy itself.

editorials.title: An $18bn settlement – and Zuckerberg barely blinked. The tech titans must be stripped of their power, and soon
editorials.passage:
F ollow the money. If you want to know how the tech giant Meta really feels about the $18bn it agreed to fork out to end a landmark lawsuit against it – an outcome widely hailed as a victory for campaigners – just look at its share price . It didn’t go down when word came on Wednesday that Meta had settled with the 29 US states that had argued that the company’s Facebook and Instagram platforms harmed children. On the contrary, Meta stock went up, initially surging by 5%, before levelling out at a gain of just over 1.25%. There could be no clearer proof that the money men reckon Meta dodged a bullet.

To be sure, there was plenty to hearten those who have long believed that social media damages teenagers especially, whether by exposing them to content they shouldn’t see or by sapping their self-esteem, offering them filters that show how much prettier they would look if they had cosmetic surgery or giving them a metric of their popularity – and unpopularity – in the form of a running tally of “likes” and views.

For one thing, $18bn is a lot of money. For another, Meta has agreed to a series of changes in the way young people use their platforms . There’ll be a two-hour daily cap on use; restricted access during the night and the school day; likes will not be shown automatically and assorted safety and parental supervision measures will no longer be opt-in extras but the default standard. You can see why Lori Schott of Colorado, who believes the content her daughter encountered on Instagram played a part in her suicide aged 18, declared Wednesday to be “a good day” .

But look closer and you see that, for Meta, $18bn is not exactly a bank-breaking sum. It amounts to less than a month’s revenue . And it has 10 years to pay it out: the monthly payments could come out of petty cash. What’s more, nearly a third of that sum is contingent on Meta’s rivals YouTube and TikTok agreeing to the same restrictions. All told, the financial penalty is less than a tenth of the $200bn the 29 states were seeking, and a tiny fraction of the $1.4tn the company told the court it feared it would have to cough up . No wonder Meta’s shareholders were doing fist bumps on Wednesday.

Beyond the money, Meta will be thankful it has escaped a court ruling against it, a legal verdict on the behaviour detailed so compellingly in the California courtroom in the first week of the trial before it was abruptly halted. Jurors heard from the former Meta safety engineer Arturo Béjar, who spoke of his own teenage daughter’s experience on Instagram – how she received unwanted sexual advances, crude misogynistic insults and photos of male genitalia on the platform – and of a survey he had conducted that found 51% of teen users had had bad or harmful experiences on Instagram within the previous seven days, and that content was taken down only 0.02% of the time. Béjar reported his findings to Mark Zuckerberg directly, but got no reply. As Béjar told me when we spoke on Thursday: “They knew that harm to kids was happening, but they were telling the world it wasn’t.” Under Wednesday’s settlement, Meta hasn’t even made an admission of liability.

As for the new restrictions, anyone who has seen a teenager on a computer or phone will have little confidence that they won’t find a way around them. If they do, then, according to this week’s deal, Meta will not be accountable. And crucially, says Béjar, it is Meta itself that still gets to define what constitutes harm.

No less frustrating, these new terms apply inside the US only, even though Meta’s reach, and its capacity to do damage, is global. As the gagged former Facebook employee Sarah Wynn-Williams described in her riveting book Careless People , the company was assiduous in hunting for new users in those overseas territories with few legal safeguards. There’s a parallel here with the tobacco industry: long after the US and Europe had cracked down on cigarettes, big tobacco was energetically selling into developing countries that had not yet put up their defences.

Above all, this week’s settlement addresses only the safety of children, despite the copious evidence of danger to adults, whether in the form of addiction or exposure to toxic misinformation. The danger lies not in this or that specific feature, but rather in the fundamental business model of social media: namely, tracking and surveilling individuals online, using the data gathered to construct a profile, which is then sold to advertisers eager to target potential consumers with extraordinary precision.

It’s this model that keeps users hooked, scrolling for hour after hour, as they are served content aimed directly at their interests and anxieties. As Ravi Naik, the lawyer who acts for Wynn-Williams and others, told me: “The algorithm preys on you.” The trouble with this latest settlement, he explains, is that “it reaches the features of Meta’s platforms but not the engine that drives them. The recommendation algorithm is untouched.”

What, then, can be done? For Béjar, the answer is to approach social media as a public health crisis, akin to the road traffic accidents that led to mandatory safety belts in cars (and not only for children). Governments need to say that any company involved in this crisis has to be involved in tackling it. And no one should fall for the line that the nature of the internet is such that it cannot be subject to meaningful regulation. When the music industry objected to copyright infringements online, incentives were swiftly arranged to fix the problem. As Béjar so damningly puts it: “A song has more protection than a kid.”

There are ample other precedents that can serve as guides to action, though none of them will please the titans of big tech. For decades, they have avoided being viewed as publishers, liable for what appears on their platforms. Nor do they want to be treated like carmakers, responsible for product safety. And they don’t like being likened to cigarette firms, selling a product they know is dangerous. Perhaps policymakers need to make a new comparison.

More than a century ago, when Standard Oil’s de facto monopoly was deemed harmful to consumers, it was broken up by order of the US supreme court into 34 smaller companies. Meta operates like a monopoly, with users feeling they can’t move, because all their friends and contacts are on the same few platforms. “Meta knowingly exploit this and refuse to make changes to their platforms that they know would deliver safer user experiences,” Damian Collins, a former chair of the UK parliamentary committee that oversees the digital realm, told me. If users could move their data and contacts over to new services, giving them more options, “break-up would work”.

This week’s settlement has been a disappointment to those longing to see the tech giants finally brought to heel, found guilty by courts and made to pay for it with costs too big to ignore. For now, Meta has swerved judgment day. But that day must surely come.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: Sunsets, disasters, dinners: we now record them all with our phones. But what is that doing to our souls?
editorials.passage:
I was sitting on a rooftop in Athens at sunset looking up at Filopappou hill. Athens in August is burning hot . Not so much hotter than London or Paris any more, but the sort of hot that makes it foolish to step out into sunlight before 6pm. Emerging from the air conditioning at dusk, I saw a dense line of silhouettes on the ridge above me. Almost every one of these shadows had its arm raised, holding a cameraphone towards the sunset.

Of all the pretty hills in the Greek capital, Filopappou arguably has the best view. The Acropolis stands directly to its north. To its south, where I sat, the city sprawls out towards the sea and a dark horizon of islands – Aegina, Salamina, Agistri.

Looking up, the wall of tourist photographers reminded me of something: war zones.

I worked as a correspondent covering conflicts and disasters for the Guardian and other newspapers for more than a decade. Over time, every new disaster came to resemble the last: another catastrophic tableau of buildings and bodies with a dense ring of telephoto lenses pointed at it.

Print reporters like me could stay at a distance from the gore and the horror because we could describe it. The photographers had to get as close as possible because they needed a clean shot.

Later, when I asked them about their work over beers at the American Colony hotel bar or tea at Gaza’s now-destroyed Al Deira hotel – how could they do it? Spend their days gazing at suffering? – most said the same thing. The lens was a buffer, a sort of protective forcefield. They weren’t looking at the fatally injured child, they were looking at the image of one.

The illustrious war photographer Don McCullin was wise to the danger in this distance. “I operate not as a photographer but as a human being,” he said in 1983, 16 years before the first cameraphone. “I try to balance what I photograph not as a photographer but as a person, a man, and photography has got nothing to do with it. It is just something I have learned, it is just a way of communicating.”

Now it’s 2026 and almost every one of us – bar the kooks and the luddites – clutches a distancing device.

I was late to Instagram , but it quickly became second nature. Now, when an attractive dish is put in front of me, an animal does something cute, a fight breaks out on a ferry, a helicopter lands to race some poor person to hospital, I pull out my phone and record it alongside everyone else.

Like the people on the hill, most of us live our lives through lenses: camera first.

And they aren’t always pointing outwards. Multi-billion-dollar industries have been built on people photographing themselves. Much has been written about the psychological perils of our narcissistic age, but increasingly, the danger is more than psychological.

Earlier this month, five teenagers were killed in a car driving the wrong way down a motorway in Ireland. They crashed into another car carrying four members of a family, all of whom were seriously injured. It seems they died taking part in an online trend in which masked young men film themselves driving recklessly at high speed, baiting police into giving chase. The camera is not incidental to the danger: the danger is created for the camera.

Forensic cyberpsychologist Mary Aiken describes this as “hybrid behaviour”: filming and driving simultaneously, with “one foot in the real world and one foot in cyberspace”. While the physical car accelerates down a motorway, part of the driver’s mind is watching the finished video, the audience, the likes from other picture-sharers around the globe.

This could also explain the fatal selfie phenomenon. A study identified 332 selfie-related deaths between 2014 and 2021, most commonly caused by drowning, falling or some form of transport. These tragedies can’t all be blamed on vanity meeting the smartphone – people have always taken stupid risks – but phone cameras have changed how we perceive danger: a cliff edge becomes a backdrop, death is content.

In Afghanistan in 2009, Associated Press photographer Julie Jacobson took nine frames over two and a half minutes of 21-year-old US L/Cpl Joshua Bernard lying fatally wounded after a Taliban ambush as he was treated by his fellow marines. Jacobson didn’t help them, she photographed.

The resulting image of Bernard’s dying face and horrific injuries provoked bitter debate. His family asked for it not to be published. The then US defence secretary, Robert Gates, called AP’s decision to release it “appalling”. The news agency argued that the photograph performed an essential public function: it forced people at home to see the reality of a war being fought in their name.

Jacobson’s defence was that in the moment she couldn’t help him and she decided the most helpful thing she could do as a photographer was to document a painful truth.

I suspect that for the average smartphone user, their cameras serve the opposite purpose. The world has become too difficult to look at directly.

Every day, those same screens show us bombed homes in Gaza, burning forests everywhere, celebrities in psychological anguish, self-harming in front of millions of TikTok followers . After reels of influencers slurping “the best cacio e pepe ever”, we are shown executions, assaults, maimed and dying children. Phone users are exposed to more suffering than a human nervous system is built to absorb, and we keep scrolling.

We’re addicted to our cameras because they have the magical capacity to turn much of what is frightening, painful or just intensely beautiful into something we can frame, edit, caption and share. They allow us to be present but absent.

It’s this sort of moral confusion I tried to explore in my novel, Vulture. Its protagonist is a British correspondent in Gaza who finds that documenting other people’s suffering gives her not only purpose but somewhere to hide. Horror becomes a picture byline; every dead body a pull quote. Bearing witness becomes absolution.

Not that we should, can or will stop recording. In Gaza, Palestinian journalists filming on their phones have provided an indispensable record of a war foreign reporters have largely been prevented from entering. There, picking up a camera is an act of extraordinary courage.

“Photography for me is not looking, it’s feeling,” the great McCullin said , an approach that has produced some of the most affecting images ever taken in conflict zones.

The rest of us may just have to work to remain human behind the lens; to remember to engage with reality once the image is posted.

Phoebe Greenwood is a former Guardian correspondent, and the author of the novel Vulture

editorials.title: Dolly Parton was the polar opposite of our bullying president
editorials.passage:
I’m still grieving Dolly Parton . I never met her and always wanted to. She was almost exactly my age and my height and had values I deeply admired. Her death leaves a hole in the firmament.

Which brings me to the person whose values are as far from Dolly Parton’s as any human could possibly be and still claim to be human. I’m referring, of course, to the current occupant of the Oval Office.

“I knew her a little bit,” Trump boasted about Parton on Glenn Beck’s radio show. “She really liked me, I will tell you!” at which Beck laughed out loud.

Trump has become mad as a hatter. Loonier than looney tunes. Totally nuts. An enraged, engorged child who’s frightened to death of being seen as a loser.

He’s losing his war in Iran – the war he decided to start without consulting Congress , without even telling the American people his goal or exit strategy.

Now he’s trapped there – with a stronger and more extreme group in control of Iran than before his attack, probably more intent on making a nuclear bomb, blocking the strait of Hormuz (it was open before Trump attacked), causing oil prices to rise again.

His current attempt to stop other countries from dealing with Iran is a bad joke. Iran is becoming the dominant power in the Gulf, having demonstrated its ability to damage the oil and gas infrastructure of its neighbors.

Besides, China can supply almost everything Iran needs and has a strong incentive to do so.

So – now clearly revealed as a loser – what does Trump do? Like any bully, he lashes out.

If the courts won’t allow him to put his name on the Kennedy Center, he’ll demolish it . If they say he doesn’t have authority to build his ballroom, he’ll fight to build it anyway .

If his blue paint on the reflecting pool is peeling and the green algae are back and his US attorney won’t prosecute “vandals” for causing the problem, he’ll stick to his story and blame vandals anyway .

It’s all going so badly for Trump that his lizard brain is compelled to show he can bully someone . So who does Trump choose? Our old neighbor and friend Canada , who has always gone along with whatever the American colossus ever wanted.

Trump imposed 50% tariffs on all cars, trucks, auto parts and steel coming from Canada.

Why? Because, he says : “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years. On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with. They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!”

In other words, we’re in a trade war with Canada because, well, Trump wants one. A trade war with Canada probably seemed easier to win than a hot war with Iran. And he had to save face somehow , right?

Even though the supreme court found his attempt to use emergency powers for his last round of tariffs to be unconstitutional , he’s now using the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 – which, not incidentally, worsened the Great Depression.

But maybe a trade war with Canada won’t be all that easy to win. Canada has now retaliated with its own tariffs of up to 50% against about 700 American products .

As the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, noted on Saturday : “Last spring, I warned that America is trying to break us so they can own us, and I promised that will never, ever happen. We are keeping that promise.”

Carney is now a hero in Canada with approval ratings in the 60s, while Trump’s have sunk to the low 30s .

Humiliation upon humiliation for the man who can’t stand to be humiliated.

It gets worse by the day.

Netanyahu has rejected Trump’s plan for Gaza. Congressional Republicans are blasting him for increasing imports of ground beef.

Universities are rejecting his latest directives. ABC has sued his regime for threatening its broadcast licenses.

Even the bond market won’t be cowed. It’s in open revolt against his bonkers fiscal policies.

Thank goodness for him that Darline Graham won South Carolina’s special election Republican runoff to replace her brother. Trump had made her race all about himself – of course – telling supporters that her opponents were “only fighting Darline because they want me to lose”.

I’m sure that’s what he’s telling himself about his many losses and humiliations – that they’re all due to his opponents plotting and scheming against him.

(Hopefully, he’s about to lose Congress, too.)

That’s an easier story for Trump to accept than the truth: that his carefully cultivated aura of invincibility has just about disappeared.

The would-be emperor has no clothes. Almost everybody now sees the thin-skinned, peevish, petty, incompetent, corrupt, naked infant who’s been parading around in presidential garb.

And they’re not going to obey him any more.

Dolly Parton was a huge winner, bless her soul. Trump is the biggest loser on the planet.

Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com . His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

editorials.title: There is clearly trouble ahead for Harry and Meghan on their return to the UK. Here are five ways to avert it
editorials.passage:
They’re back! Harry and Meghan’s quiet return to England this week, via Birmingham airport , was much anticipated but scarcely celebrated – no bunting or street parties.

So far there are many questions but very few answers: not just “why return now?” and “why so suddenly?”, but also questions of security: who pays if not themselves, given that they are not working royals? And where will the money come from to keep them in the style to which they are accustomed?

The bills are mounting: not just the Daily Mail’s legal costs incurred by Harry’s ill-fated court action, but even the upkeep of their nine-bedroom Montecito mansion, which, with property taxes, mortgage and upkeep (including looking after their chickens), could cost about $80,000 (£60,000) a month . That’s to say nothing about the house in Portugal . Meghan will have to get some pretty meaty and regular acting jobs – and fast.

Maybe all will be well, they will readjust to British life and Britain will readjust to them, but on past experience this seems highly unlikely. Can they avert it? Here are five tips that might help.

1. Find capable advisers. Not necessarily the pin-striped courtiers who serve at the palace and know a great deal but whom Harry hated, nor the subversives like Mark Bolland , the PR guru , who once advised Charles as prince and seems to have initiated rows with half the rest of the family. Young smart-alec briefers are not required, nor perhaps Americans who don’t have a feel for Britain and its generally pro-royalist population. There are considerable bridges to be rebuilt with the people who feel Harry and Meghan let them down, and especially with the rest of the royal family. The couple need careful guidance over how they should present themselves, when they should speak and what they should say – or not say. No more interviews with Oprah Winfrey slagging off the relatives. It makes a splash, but thereafter, it doesn’t exactly help.

2. Make peace again with the family, especially William and Catherine. It may be difficult and arduous to restore trust, but they need to do that as quickly as possible. And no setting up a rival court: they must know by now the obligation to choose discreet friends wisely.

3. Help out a bit. Not necessarily with the washing-up but with attendance at public events, visits and charities. Not by freeloading, the public hates that, but by generally doing good – not for a few minutes or a day or two between flips to California, but regularly and humbly.

4. Breathe deeply and make nice with the media – and not just the networks that have previously been prepared to pay them mega money. Wiser members of the royal family face challenges too, but they know that they need the so-called dead tree media, including newspapers, for their popularity. A smile goes further than a snarl. Remember that you need them more than they need you – they have businesses to run, you have a public perception to shape via their products. If they stop reporting on the royals or all the coverage is negative, the institution’s days of crisis will never end.

Think hard about what to communicate and what you try to keep secret. The “secret” – private – christening of Archie was unnecessary as was William’s attempt to hide the name of a family dog from an avid press and public. The media will always ferret even more important things out – such as their new home and the children’s school (especially if, as reported, Harry wants to watch young Archie play rugby every Saturday ) and a defensive, sneering approach gains nothing. It just makes ever-fragile media/royal relations even worse. Better to be as open as possible and broker an arrangement for the media to thereafter leave Archie and Lilibet alone – it has worked for William and Catherine’s children. Harry and Meghan must face up to the fact they will always be newsworthy and isn’t that partly what they want to publicise their ventures?

5. Above all, smile, for God’s sake. Harry and Meghan are both in a very privileged position. People won’t like it if they appear to despise or patronise them, or to feel too sorry for themselves. They have the opportunity to be identified with the great cause of cheering people up. Cometh the hour … perhaps.

Steve Bates is a former Guardian royal correspondent

editorials.title: The hill I will die on: The barbecue is fundamentally unenjoyable. Please, put a lid on it
editorials.passage:
“I f you’re invited to a barbecue, have your dinner before you go.” It is the wisest advice my dad has ever given me. Barbecues are one of life’s perennial disappointments. The romance of eating outside quickly degenerates into a recipe for mucky fingers, smelly clothes and more mess than you bargained for , with grills that you can never get clean, uncomfortable seating that makes your back ache or, dafter still, eating while standing up. Worst of all is the true barbecue legacy – the nagging hunger that follows bitty dining, leaving you with the aggrieved sense that you missed a mealtime you’re never getting back.

I grew up in Cornwall, where beach barbecues were a rite of passage. The flame under the sandy grill was blown out by the Atlantic wind, so these gatherings were impractical, unpredictable and interminable. One minute the sausages were raw and looked like they’d never be ready, the next they were hard and black and basically inedible. Rain frequently sent us scrambling to pack up and flee for shelter.

Even when it doesn’t rain, and the scene is a suburban garden where something that looks like it belongs in a gastropub kitchen has been installed to char halloumi three times a year, I find myself wondering: “How is this fun?” Barbecues are terrible for socialising because the food trickles out, with kids served first (why, when they have the most energy?), so guests don’t eat at the same time and instead dine in silos, wondering if they’ll get home early enough to make pasta. As for drinks, they’re warm because ice buckets don’t work – they’re too small and the ice melts almost instantly in the kind of temperatures we’ve seen this summer – and nobody wants to dash back and forth to the fridge.

The popularity of barbecues is inexplicable yet undeniable, with black smoke puffing from back gardens at the first sniff of a sunny day. When I broached my hatred with an Australian, she reacted as if I wanted to deprive her of her birthright. But just because people keep doing something doesn’t necessarily mean they actually enjoy it.

Barbecues are antisocial in other, more important ways. I used to live above a man who liked to come home from work and barbecue steak on his patio, directly below my kitchen. I had to close every window to stop my whole flat stinking of beef. If you live in a densely populated area, it’s not particularly socially conscious to fill the air with meaty smog during hot weather, just so you can clog your arteries.

Disposable barbecues, which have been factors in wildfires during this summer’s heatwaves, are the worst. This month, one caused a forest fire in the North York Moors , while Dorset and Wiltshire fire and rescue recently told people to go to the pub instead . A spokesperson added: “I’d certainly challenge anybody to say whether they’ve ever had a good meal from a disposable barbecue.” An excellent point which, if we’re honest, applies to all variations of barbecue.

Max Liu is a freelance writer
