editorials.title: ‘Once Elephants Lived Here’: Geetanjali Shree’s stories play with ideas and readers’ expectations
editorials.passage:
There is an intriguing instability in the world of Once Elephants Lived Here . The stories start out in places that seem familiar, with characters you have run into variations of already, until suddenly, the real morphs into the fantastic.

A strangely expansive sky turns into a lover. An ambitious young man attempts to find his place in a city that has cleaved into two. A woman starts her morning with a routine walk and cannot stop. A man sits in his friend’s house, waiting anxiously, watching shadows. A couple finds the beginning and the end of their love story in a graveyard. A mother finds joy in sakura blossoms, millions of miles away from home. With the surreal skirting the edges of everyday existence in contemporary spaces, these stories defy easy classification and easy consumption. They unfold across a range of settings – a city that promises to be a superpower, a village that has not let go of older ways of life, a generic housing society, a beautiful hamlet in Kerala, a new planet, an ordinary hotel room, a train in Japan. Their concerns are just as varied. Like the rest of Geetanjali Shree’s fiction, this anthology of 11 stories, first published in 2012 as Yahan Haathi Rahtey Thhey and translated from the Hindi by Daisy Rockwell, explores the complexities of human behaviour. Each of the stories in this selection plays with form, ideas, and, decisively, with the reader’s expectations.

The eponymous story, set in a town that has lost its memories of the past, introduces the reader to an old woman: “Wherever she appeared, she was an unusual sight, but at the same time, she was supremely ordinary. Wherever she showed up was not her place, but it became her place. She could be anywhere, could belong anywhere. She belonged where she was today, and she'd belong where she appeared tomorrow.” The woman, never named, is the first of the many “complex elderly characters” Rockwell identifies as a recurring presence in Shree’s fiction. The town stands bifurcated into inviolable halves and has no place for the old. They are relegated to silence, removed from both public spaces and public discourse. The old woman remains unmoved by these codes. She becomes a story, a legend, powerful in the way stories are, reminding those who would rather forget that the past can never be permanently erased.

In sharp contrast to her self-assured reclamation of space and time is the cantankerous father in “The End”. In the manner of ageing patriarchs everywhere, he continues to make his children and his wife miserable with his excessive calls on their time, labour and attention. And then there is the enigmatic grandfather in “And I Saw Myself Running”. Larger than life, Baba holds his household, his community and the entire village in thrall. He has the power to control snakes, much as he controls people, holding them under his protection while also entertaining himself at their expense. Baba is so authoritarian, time seems to bend to his will. Aggressively masculine, he reduces the narrator to a childlike state of indecision and insignificance. Age, in these stories, does not adhere to conventional narratives of effacement. It is deviously defiant, and the aged, engagingly anomalous.

The world of this collection has the same jagged edges as our own. The city of “Once Elephants Lived Here” has been sculpted by riots: “The riots made this city famous. Well, not the riots themselves but the glitter and glamour that most definitely resulted from the riots.” The text does not spell it out but clues are scattered all over, coaxing the involved reader to connect the dots between rioting, a river that divides an erstwhile composite space and composite people, two factions on either side of the recently drawn-up border and the implied safety in living with people of your own kind.

The trauma of the Partition lives on, 80 years after its genesis. Its violent legacy echoes in “These Days”, where a man, making an obvious show of being Hindu, adjusting to the optics of “looking” his religious identity by shaving off his beard and performing regular puja for the benefit of his neighbours, sits in the literal glare of headlights so as to show himself as harmless; someone who deserves the protection of the community. The house he occupies belongs to his friend, a Muslim, who, to take his own belongings, must break into his home under the cover of darkness, taking the form of shadows. In this city beset by communal violence, community has broken down and the only time anyone sees other people is when curfew is relaxed for a few hours. The narrative builds up anxiety and tension as the man waits, his inaction an obvious reminder of his loss of agency, echoing an essential psycho-social truth of our times. The woman who goes on a morning walk and finds herself unable to stop in “Out for a Spin” also draws attention to the sterility of urban spaces – posh housing societies, neighbourhood parks, community spaces – that have become sites of observation and even surveillance but have lost all human connection. No one hears her, no one pays attention, no one attempts to help. The critique is as damning as it is subtle.

Women in Geetanjali Shree’s fiction have often been subversive in unexpected ways. The pattern remains unbroken here. In “Echo”, a middle-aged woman, rekindling a “bygone college romance” in a nondescript hotel room in a nondescript city, refuses to give up first dibs to the newspaper. “I’ve never understood why men are such newspaper-worshippers”, she says. “For my father, it – the newspaper – was like a breast for a baby. It appeared before dawn – tea banana biscuit newspaper – presented on a tray as a small offering one might serve a sahib and a nawab.” It is as though in claiming control over the newspaper, men, across generations, claim control over the world, establishing their natural supremacy over all they survey. The woman resists. She spars with her new romantic partner, not ceding an inch, even when it threatens their relationship.

The morning walker in “Out for a Spin” is a writer who started going for a walk while it was still dark because to be seen by the society residents was to be labelled interminably. “We are revealed in the eyes of others”, she insists. The world outside is always pointing fingers and yelling: “Madam, your bra strap is slipping, your hair is turning white, your belly insists on protruding through your clothing, and what outlandish thing you are wearing anyway, not feminine, not masculine, not Eastern or Western!” Caught in a loop of incessant, involuntary movement that pushes her into public view, the gazes on her reveal the ways in which the world looks at her, undermines her, and packs her away as an aberration that is best ignored.

“So Much Sky” has another writer, another middle-aged woman, in conflict with the government, the way artists, globally, often seem to be. She is sent on a writer’s retreat by the same government (as a peaceful act of distancing?), and finds herself in a new world, a world run by bots and automation, a world where the sky is endless and playful and alive. In a radical break from the rituals and reality of the Anthropocene, the woman and the sky fall in love. “It wasn’t magic, but it was definitely magical”, is how she describes it. That is also exactly how the reader receives the story – as not quite magic but definitely magical. Something of the same shade of magical spills into “March, Ma and Sakura”, where a young man working in Japan is anxious about his visiting mother’s ability to navigate a new country and culture. As the sakura blossoms, so does Ma. Witnessing her changing her usual saree for more practical clothes, making new friends, learning to map the city, unsettles him. Her freedom is agonising to him: “There was nothing I could do. Ma had slipped through my fingers, like those sparkling grains of sand.” Patriarchy, in the form of sons and lovers and society, will continue to want to police women’s bodies, their choices, and their joy, these stories seem to say, and women, in fiction and elsewhere, will continue to live with defiance.

In an interesting stylistic choice, many of Shree’s protagonists remain unnamed. The lack of a name seems to preserve each character in a private space of their own. Withholding a little something from the reader, they become a little more human, a little more real, shifting beyond the cognitive into the affective. In “Butterflies”, the narrator is a writer, grieving a personal loss in Kerala, “a place of matchless beauty”, where, despite the barrier of language, she begins to forge new connections with a set of young girls, as fragile and as doomed as they are full of hope. “Bulldozer”, set in Japan, runs through divergent landscapes and temporalities, delving into the narrator’s idyllic childhood in Ranikhet and juxtaposing it against the sharp anxiety of a train journey she took a year ago, hoping to catch sight of the sublimity of Mount Fuji. Both stories, as also the aforementioned “And I Saw Myself Running” and “Once Elephants Lived Here”, turn on memory, that elusive trickster that cares nothing for truth-telling. Affect – a recognition of loss, an anticipation of the end, an inexplicable fear, an untold history – becomes the only lens through which these narratives coalesce.

In her Translator’s Note, Rockwell refers to translation as “a form of commentary or interpretation”. As a reader with access to the translation as well as the source text, it would be disingenuous to not explore the obvious synergy between the two. Rockwell’s translation stands tall as an independent text that must adhere to its own stylistic imperatives. In “So Much Sky”, she excises what she identifies as a “framing story” involving an email, the image of Rabindranath Tagore, and mind-reading tricks, calling attention to the praxis of translation and the undeniability of the untranslatable – an idea or an image that remains impossible to re-situate and re-contextualise.

Shree’s Hindi is peppered with words from English, adopting a conversational tonality that signifies a post-colonial loosening of linguistic boundaries. Rockwell’s translation pushes the bilingual reader towards the source text. Once you get there, you run into strange little stories, told remarkably well, and a prose marked by its lightness of hand, its ability to converse. In both the source text and this impressive translation, the reader, like the woman who fell in love with the sky, is sure to find something that isn’t magic, but is definitely magical.

Once Elephants Lived Here: Stories, Geetanjali Shree, translated from the Hindi by Daisy Rockwell, Penguin India.

editorials.title: Dimagi Naxals? The sages of the Vedas and the Upanishads would qualify today
editorials.passage:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s newly minted phrase dimagi Naxal – “intellectual Naxal” – is meant to designate an ideological enemy: people whose ideas supposedly endanger the nation by questioning its political direction.

In his Independence Day address this year, Modi warned that although armed Naxalism was nearing its end, its ideological adherents are still a threat. Critics immediately pointed out the phrase’s obvious affinity with the government’s earlier use of the phrase “urban Naxal” to stigmatise academics, activists, intellectuals, and other dissenting voices.

There is, however, an unintended irony in this language. If dimagi Naxal is to mean someone who questions authority, then some of the earliest and most formidable dimagi Naxals in India were the sages who composed the Vedas and Upanishads – texts that the Hindutva brigade claims as the philosophical wellspring of their ideology.

Just last year, at an event in Ahmedabad, Home Minister Amit Shah shared his post-retirement plans: to study the Vedas and the Upanishads. While this interest in India’s ancient texts may appear commendable, a closer look at Vedic literature reveals a complex, pluralistic, and heterodox tradition that is fundamentally at odds with the ideology that Shah and his associates champion.

The regular appeal to the Vedic tradition by the Bharatiya Janata Party and its parent, the Rashtriya Swayansevak Sangh, in order to legitimise a Hindu nationalist agenda is more than a cultural fantasy: it has gone hand-in-hand with a political vision in which dissent is equated with treason, and pluralism with weakness.

Since coming to power in 2014, the BJP-led government has been increasingly criticised for marginalising religious minorities and muzzling press freedom. Voices that question the government have been trolled as “anti-national”, “sickular”, “tukde-tukde gang”, “urban Naxal” and now “dimaagi Naxal.”

However, should Modi or Shah seriously engage with the Vedas in search of validation for the Hindutva project, they may find themselves disappointed. The Vedas and the Upanishads, far from offering uncritical support to religious dogma and philosophical certitude, constitute the foundation of a long tradition of rigorous argumentation, critique, and scepticism – even about the gods.

Consider, for instance, the famous Nasadiya Sukta from the oldest extant Sanskrit text, the Rig Veda , composed circa mid-2nd millennium BCE. This creation hymn speculates on various paradoxical possibilities for the origins of the cosmos, before culminating in a profound doubt about whether even the gods possess such knowledge:

“…Whence is this creation? The gods came afterwards, with the creation of this universe. Who then knows whence it has arisen?

Whence this creation has arisen – perhaps it formed itself, or perhaps it did not – the one who looks down on it, in the highest heaven, only he knows or perhaps he does not know.”

This radical questioning of the gods is deepened in the Upanishads, composed from around the 8th century BCE. The oldest and longest of them, the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad , for instance, not only displays a spirit of irreverence towards the gods but actively urges seekers not to venerate them as powers external to the self.

One of the principal ideas developed in the Upanishads is the oneness of atman (the self) and brahman (absolute reality). This knowledge reveals a profound unity with the cosmos, leading to compassion for all beings. In this state, the gods become dispensable, as the self is understood to be one with them.

“Yet, as the Brihadaranyaka warns, the gods – driven by their hunger for power – seek to withhold this knowledge from humans: If a man knows ‘I am brahman ’ in this way, he becomes the whole world. Not even the gods are able to prevent it, for he becomes their very self ( atman ). So when a man venerates another deity, thinking, ‘He is one, and I am another,’ he does not understand. … The gods are not pleased at the prospect of men coming to understand this.”

This passage portrays the gods as dependent on human ignorance for their power, as insecure beings protective of their status, and as fearful of human enlightenment. The Upanishads consistently engage in such trenchant power critique, as is also evidenced from several philosophical disputes voiced in the texts.

We find one such debate in Chapter 3 of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad where the sage Yajnavalkya fields profound metaphysical questions from a range of scholars, including Gargi Vachaknavi, a woman who not only challenges Yajnavalkya’s wisdom but also mocks him repeatedly for his opaque explanations.

This tradition of intellectual contestation and public debate stands in sharp contrast with the atmosphere of censorship and religio-moral policing enabled by the Modi-Shah regime – not to mention the glaring absence of accountability to a free press, with the prime minister refusing to address a single press conference since taking office.

Similarly, while the last decade has seen Hindutva goons frequently lynching individuals suspected of eating beef, the Vedas clearly portray a society where eating cow-meat was common practice both in sacrificial feasts like the gomedha and in social ceremonies like weddings and funerals, as several verses in the Rig Veda indicate.

Even Swami Vivekananda attested to this fact, when he wrote that according to ancient scriptures, “he is not a good Hindu who does not eat beef” ( Complete Works , Vol. 3, “Buddhistic India”).

The RSS-BJP’s appropriation of ancient India is not only intellectually dishonest but also corrosive to the country’s historically diverse and secular social fabric.

Of course, the Vedas, like all ancient texts, are deeply flawed. They do contain hierarchical ideas, such as varna, which later consolidated into caste oppression. Yet they also offer fertile ground for multiple contesting – even contradictory – narratives to coexist and thrive.

If the sages who composed these texts were alive today, they would certainly have faced the ire of the government, vilified on social media for questioning the status quo, and perhaps been labeled dimagi Naxals.

Tuhin Bhattacharjee is an assistant professor in the department of philosophy at DePaul University in Chicago.

editorials.title: JudgeGPT: AI has entered active justice delivery
editorials.passage:
Anyone who has dealt with the Indian judiciary is often left wondering why the system so often resembles a Bangalore traffic jam that never seems to clear for timely justice. A legal dispute can remain alive for years while the circumstances that created it change completely. Property loses value, businesses move on, families exhaust their resources and people grow old waiting for a judgment. A democracy cannot treat timely justice as an administrative luxury. Rights have little practical force when the machinery meant to enforce them moves too slowly.

The scale of India’s judicial backlog is difficult to ignore. As of March 9, 2026, 64,01,789 cases were pending in the High Courts and 4,95,49,089 in subordinate courts. The Supreme Court had 92,621 pending cases as of March 13, 2026. Together, the three levels account for more than 5.5 crore pending cases. The numbers point to a capacity problem that extends beyond the number of judges. Courts must absorb enormous volumes of documents, precedents, pleadings and procedural information before a judge can reach the question that actually matters: what does justice require in this case?

That informational burden is where AI becomes relevant. AI cannot decide what justice means, and it should not decide it. At least not at this juncture, when AI isn’t conscious and its capabilities aren’t consistently reliable. It can, however, reduce the time a judge spends searching, sorting and summarising information. A lot of legal work and effort is spent on precisely these activities.

A large-scale experiment in Pakistan provides a useful indication of what is becoming possible with advancing technology. The country deployed an AI system called JudgeGPT to assist trial judges with legal research and judgment preparation. The system combined GPT-4 with a database containing 128,292 Pakistani judicial opinions and 943 statutes. Using retrieval-augmented generation, it could surface relevant authorities and connect its responses to the underlying legal sources.

The results were measurable. Districts participating in the programme recorded a 6.3 per cent increase in cases resolved, with no obvious decline in judgement quality. Appeal rates also fell slightly. By the time 487 judges had received the specialised training, the median district had recorded this increase in case resolution, and the effect was larger where more judges had been trained. The researchers estimated that a trained judge was resolving 38.5 more cases a month than the baseline.

These gains should be interpreted as an early-stage baseline rather than a ceiling. As with any new tool, initial adoption is constrained by learning curves and workflow adjustment. Productivity typically improves as users gain familiarity and integrate the system more naturally into routine work.

A 6.3 per cent improvement will not clear India’s backlog quickly. That is the wrong benchmark. The significance of the Pakistani experiment is that a modest increase in judicial productivity can be produced by changing how judges interact with legal information. At India’s scale, even small gains become institutionally significant if they can be reproduced across thousands of courts.

The experiment also exposes an assumption that has shaped legal institutions for decades: that judicial capacity is largely determined by the number of people available to do the work. A judge who can find a relevant precedent in seconds rather than spending hours searching through case law has more time available for reasoning. A judge who receives a reliable summary of a lengthy record can spend more time examining disputed evidence. A judge who can retrieve the relevant statutory provisions quickly does not become an AI judge; the judge simply begins the human part of adjudication with better access to information.

The possibilities extend beyond legal research. An Indian judicial AI system could reconstruct the chronology of a case, identify the principal disputed facts, summarise arguments from both sides and map the relevant statutes and precedents. It could flag citations that require verification and identify whether a judgment has subsequently been modified or overruled. It could turn oral proceedings into searchable transcripts and help court registries identify cases that have remained inactive or have been repeatedly adjourned.

That would move AI from a document-search tool to part of the operating infrastructure of justice. The greatest opportunity may therefore lie outside the final judgment itself. AI can help courts manage the information surrounding a case so that judicial attention is directed towards questions that require human judgment.

India has already started building the digital foundations for this shift. The National Judicial Data Grid provides a national platform for judicial data, while the Supreme Court has explored AI-enabled transcription and other technology-assisted functions. The judiciary has also been examining broader frameworks for responsible AI adoption. These developments suggest that the question is no longer whether technology belongs in the justice system. The more consequential question is where AI should be permitted to operate and under what controls.

The controls cannot be an afterthought. The Pakistan study found that judges who received specialised training used JudgeGPT far more consistently than those who received generic technology training. It also found that roughly one-fifth of prompts involved substantial AI delegation, including requests for legal reasoning or recommendations about the appropriate decision. Training reduced inappropriate delegation.

India should take that warning seriously. A judicial AI system cannot operate like a general-purpose chatbot. It should be connected to authenticated statutes, judgments, procedural rules and official court records. Legal claims generated by the system should carry verifiable sources. The system should maintain an audit trail of its contribution. Judges should be able to distinguish between retrieved authority and generated analysis. Most importantly, responsibility for the judgment must remain with the judge.

There is another reason to move carefully. The underlying research argues that AI can make litigation cheaper and, in some circumstances, reduce the incentive for parties to settle. When the cost of going to trial falls, both sides may become more willing to pursue litigation. The result could be more cases reaching court even as each case becomes cheaper to process.

This matters greatly for India. The objective cannot simply be to make courts process more cases faster. AI should be used to identify where cases can be resolved earlier, where procedural bottlenecks are creating delays and where mediation or settlement could prevent unnecessary litigation. A faster judicial system that merely produces a faster queue is not a complete solution.

The deeper issue is democratic. Legislatures can create rights relatively quickly. Courts give those rights practical force. When judicial remedies take years, the distance between constitutional promise and lived reality grows. The citizen may technically possess a right while lacking a timely mechanism to enforce it.

That is why AI has become difficult to keep at the margins of justice delivery. The technology is already capable of handling substantial parts of the information-processing work surrounding adjudication. The Pakistani experiment demonstrates that even an early implementation can produce measurable gains when the technology is connected to authoritative legal material and judges are properly trained.

India should therefore stop asking whether AI can replace judges. That is the wrong question. The useful question is how much unnecessary cognitive and administrative work can be removed from a judge’s day without transferring judicial responsibility to a machine.

The answer will determine whether AI becomes another layer of court technology or a genuine instrument of judicial reform. Machines can search millions of pages, organise evidence and retrieve precedent at a scale no individual judge can match. Judges must decide what those materials mean, weigh competing claims and remain accountable for the consequences of their decisions.

India’s judicial AI policy should therefore be built around a simple institutional principle: automate information processing, strengthen judicial reasoning and keep accountability human. The success of JudgeGPT should not be measured by how much technology a court deploys. It should be measured by whether citizens spend less of their lives waiting for justice.

(Sreejith Sreedharan is a technology analyst and author of ‘Future of Work – AI Augmented Autonomous Decentralised’. He works on organisational AI readiness and created the AI Instinct Index®, a psychometric diagnostic designed to assess behavioural readiness for AI adoption and adaptive capacity in constraint-heavy environments. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Nepal disaster is a warning: The Himalayas are changing in dangerous ways
editorials.passage:
The catastrophic flood which descended through the Nepal Himalayas this week will inevitably revive discussion about Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs). That is useful, but it should lead us towards a more comprehensive understanding of what is happening in the high mountains.

A GLOF is only one member of a growing family of Himalayan hazards.

Glaciers can retreat and leave expanding lakes behind them. Moraine dams can fail. Hanging glaciers can detach. Entire masses of rock and ice can break away from steep mountain faces. Permafrost which has helped bind high-altitude rock together can degrade. One event can trigger another, converting an avalanche into a debris flow, temporarily damming a river and eventually producing a catastrophic flood hundreds of kilometres downstream.

That appears increasingly close to the sequence now emerging from Nepal.

 
When the Mountain Itself Moves
Early reports suggested that an earthquake may have triggered the collapse of the glacier. That interpretation has changed significantly as more evidence has emerged.

The US Geological Survey now assesses that the seismic signal initially interpreted as an earthquake was generated by the glacial collapse and debris flow itself. The event released energy equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. A huge mass of rock and ice detached from the glaciated face of Langtang Lirung, descended more than a kilometre and entered the river system below. The resulting debris flow and flood travelled down the river valley.

Estimates of the dimensions will inevitably be refined. Satellite analysis suggests that the glacier lost an area equivalent to roughly 25 professional football fields, while specialists analysing the seismic signature estimate that perhaps 50–100 million cubic metres of material may have been involved. The numbers are almost difficult to visualise. The physics is easier.

If millions of tons of ice and rock are stored high above a steep valley, gravity provides enormous potential energy. Release the mass suddenly and the descending fragments entrain rock, soil, snow and water, and can transform themselves into something resembling moving concrete. In the Chamoli disaster at Tapovan in February 2021, an event I physically investigated, the adjoining area up to three kilometres on either side of the icefall witnessed the uprooting of massive trees due to the unprecedented air current. The cascading effect downstream becomes progressively worse.

The narrow Himalayan valley becomes the easiest route downhill. Unfortunately, it is also where roads, bridges, hydropower projects, settlements, administrative and military posts, tourists and pilgrims tend to be concentrated.

 
Beyond the Familiar GLOF
We have become accustomed to using GLOF almost as shorthand for glacier-related flooding. Technically, that can be misleading. A classic GLOF occurs when water accumulated in a glacial lake is suddenly released, often following failure of the moraine or other material containing it.

South Lhonak in Sikkim in October 2023 is an obvious recent example, although even in that case the process was more complex than simply a lake “bursting”. Recent research indicates that a landslide deposited an enormous quantity of material into the lake, accompanied by the breaking away, or ‘calving’, of a substantial mass of glacial ice into the lake. The resulting waves contributed to the failure of the moraine and the devastating flood downstream.

Rishiganga-Tapovan in Uttarakhand in February 2021 was different. There was no cloudburst on that clear winter morning and no conventional GLOF. A massive rock-and-ice avalanche descended from Ronti Peak and transformed into an extraordinarily destructive debris flow.

The distinction matters because we cannot build an effective warning architecture if we assume that all high-mountain floods originate in the same manner.

 
The Permafrost Question
There is another word which needs to enter India’s public discussion on Himalayan hazards: permafrost. Permafrost is ground — soil, sediment or rock — which remains frozen for at least two consecutive years. In high mountains, ice within cracks and fractures can effectively help bind rock masses together.

As temperatures rise and freeze-thaw cycles change, that binding can weaken. Retreating glaciers also remove support from adjoining mountain slopes and expose rock previously protected by ice. Water can penetrate fractures, freeze, thaw and progressively weaken the mountain structure. The result is not that mountains suddenly become unstable everywhere. That would be alarmist. It means that particular high-altitude slopes may become more susceptible to failure.

This is an emerging area of Himalayan science. Recent research into the western Himalayas notes that detailed understanding of permafrost distribution and its degradation remains limited. Significantly, more than 70 per cent of documented rock-ice avalanches across High Mountain Asia have originated in zones considered likely to contain permafrost. It deserves much greater attention.

 
The Cascading Hazard
The real challenge is not individual hazards but cascades. A warming mountain face can lose stability. Rock and ice collapse. An avalanche may strike a glacial lake and generate an enormous displacement wave. It may block a river temporarily. Water accumulates behind the debris. The improvised dam then fails. The flood entrains still more rock, soil and vegetation as it descends.

By the time it reaches habitation, what began as an ice or rock failure kilometres away may appear to those downstream simply as an inexplicable wall of mud and water.

This also explains why immediate attribution after Himalayan disasters is hazardous. Cloudburst is frequently the first explanation because intense rainfall is familiar and intuitively understandable. Scientific evidence often arrives later. Disaster management therefore needs humility alongside technology; first establish what happened, then understand why.

 
Watching the Mountains Differently
India’s remote-sensing capability has improved enormously. NRSC’s ability to compare satellite imagery before and after events is giving scientists extraordinary insights into glacier behaviour, glacial lakes and high-altitude terrain.

The next step must increasingly be to convert observation into warning. Sensors measuring lake levels, ground movement, temperature and seismic activity will become increasingly important. So will AI-assisted interpretation of satellite and sensor data. Yet technology need not exclude simple measures. A GLOF mitigation programme set up by the government is undertaking a wide range of measures to identify and mitigate the threats in different zones.

During my association with disaster management, I had suggested that major projects located in vulnerable mountain valleys should consider trained physical observation upstream, backed by reliable and redundant communications. Experienced mountain men positioned at carefully selected locations may sometimes detect abnormal river behaviour, unusual sounds, debris movement or other warning signs before sophisticated information reaches a project site.

Thirty minutes can empty a construction site. An hour can save hundreds of lives. The concept is not technology versus human observation. It is redundancy, and one is glad to see it is increasingly being adopted.

 
Mapping the Consequence, Not Just the Hazard
Our hazard maps too must evolve. Identifying an unstable glacier, expanding lake or vulnerable mountain face is only the beginning. We must trace the entire probable downstream pathway — settlements, bridges, tunnels, hydropower installations, pilgrimage routes and other concentrations of people which may lie in its path. The concept of mapping information, so familiar to military men, must be adopted. Perfect prediction is well-nigh impossible; the Himalayas will never permit that.

There must be progressively better understanding of where instability exists, how one hazard can cascade into another, where the resulting energy will travel and how quickly information can reach those in its path.

The Nepal tragedy is another reminder that Himalayan hazards are becoming more complex, and that familiar explanations may no longer suffice.

We may not always know when or where the next event will occur. But every improvement in understanding gives us a better chance of recognising the danger a little earlier. In disaster management, knowledge acquires its greatest value when it buys time. And time saves lives.

(The author is Governor of Bihar, former Member of NDMA and former Commander of India’s Srinagar-based Chinar Corps. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Bangladesh’s Islamist drift: India needs a new Dhaka strategy
editorials.passage:
An ill wind is rising in the east. Bangladesh, a delta nation of more than 170 million people, projected to reach 200 million in the next two decades, has developed strategic amnesia and is becoming a breeding ground for the Islamic brotherhood and beyond.

Today, Islamic parties are in a decisive position both politically and in Bangladeshi society. This rising Islamic fervour is a clear and present danger; indeed, a global menace to secularism. This is Hamas on steroids. Yet all is not lost, for India is in the way.

Bangladesh, for a start, is hemmed in on three sides by India. The Islamic Jamaat dreams of the chicken’s neck, yet forgets that India can slice through the whole roast in a jhatka. Political reaction to a jihadi surge in Bangladesh is inevitable.

If political competition in Bangladesh were to culminate in the accession of Islamist forces to power, the consequences would extend beyond the immediate electoral arena. Resistance could emerge from both of the country’s principal political parties, while the military would remain a consequential institutional actor in determining the limits of this political change. It has ruled Bangladesh with an iron hand in the past and could step out of the barracks again.

The possibility of an Islamist government could therefore produce a contest not merely over office but over the constitutional and institutional character of the state. Under such conditions, political instability would arise from the interaction between electoral legitimacy and an Islamist mandate. This would be met with counter-partisan mobilisation and the military’s historically significant role in Bangladesh’s political order.

The international dimension may prove equally consequential. If external powers and domestic centres of authority came to regard an Islamist government as incompatible with the national interest and regional stability, they might increasingly consider a military-mediated alternative, drawing on the Egyptian precedent in which military intervention prevented the Muslim Brotherhood from consolidating political power.

Such a response is not far-fetched and would expose a fundamental dilemma for democratic politics: international actors may endorse democratic procedures while simultaneously becoming less tolerant of democratic outcomes perceived as strategically destabilising. Across Islamic polities, a difficult test lingers: whether democracy can remain an unconditional organising principle when its possible outcomes conflict with the security preferences of powerful domestic and international actors.

With India, Dhaka is on a crash course. So far, India is doing the right thing by speaking softly. Yet India has a big stick it can wield. Since the upheaval that drove Sheikh Hasina from power in August 2024, Dhaka has treated New Delhi’s overtures with a mixture of scorn, suspicion and calculated distance.

India, on her part, has so far been tolerant, giving only a few slaps on the wrist. Visa services were suspended and only partially restored after prolonged friction. Preferential access and practical arrangements that once eased Bangladeshi garment exports through Indian facilities were scaled back. The long-stalled Teesta water-sharing formula remains unsigned, while the 1996 Ganges Treaty edges towards expiry in December 2026. It’s here that India could begin going beyond wrist-slapping.

India may well scrap the treaty that robs Bihar of its just share of waters.

 
The stalling economy
Bangladesh is a stubborn ‘one-trick donkey’. With the Bangladeshi economy strained, ready-made garments still account for roughly four-fifths of merchandise exports and employ six million people directly. The problem is that textiles are not exactly rocket science; there is no real moat.

For Dhaka, economic diversification has remained aspirational for decades; non-garment manufactured exports have never achieved critical mass. After Hasina’s fall, official growth figures tell a sad story. Fiscal year 2023-24 closed with growth below 4 per cent. This, according to successive Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics revisions, is the weakest performance outside the pandemic.

India could cut higher-end textile exports from Bangladesh. India’s garment exports are rising on the back of the Free Trade Agreement and cheaper electricity. India’s textile and apparel market grew to $190 billion in 2025-26 and is projected to reach $350 billion by 2030. It needs an industrial policy that can cut out the value-added textile business of Bangladesh. A policy that will have much more impact than defence spending can. If India continues to take a meaningful share of Bangladesh’s exports, it will hamper the Islamic threat too.

And as the Muslim Brotherhood rises, that threat becomes more real. Groups long constrained under Hasina — Jamaat-e-Islami Bangladesh, Hefazat-e-Islam, Ansar al-Islam, Jamaat-ul-Mujahideen Bangladesh and the neo-variant, Hizb-ut-Tahrir, Harkat-ul-Jihad al-Islami Bangladesh — have moved from the margins towards open reorganisation. Jamaat, banned and its leaders prosecuted for wartime massacres and rapes that badly bequeathed Bangladesh with millions of kids, saw its proscription lifted. Its student wing has been warmly received in campus unions once considered secular strongholds. Hefazat has staged large rallies demanding the restoration of “absolute trust and faith in Allah”.

The problem is it’s not a Bengali calling but a Punjabi one! Meanwhile, Ansar al-Islam, linked to al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent, and residual JMB networks have benefited from jailbreaks during the 2024 disorder and from subsequent bail decisions that returned experienced cadres to the streets. Hizb-ut-Tahrir has shifted from clandestine study circles to public “March for Khilafah” processions. Parallel to these domestic shifts runs a quieter network with Pakistan-based organisations. Intelligence assessments and open-source reporting point to renewed contacts between local cells and Lashkar-e-Taiba facilitators. India has some breaks, including from Afghan Taliban circles.

Bangladesh’s own history supplies a cautionary mirror. The country was not born because Islam required more territory; it was born because the Islamic unity promised in 1947 proved a fiction under Punjabi military and bureaucratic dominance. The 1970 election victory of the Awami League was simply refused. Independence in December 1971 was therefore a rejection of that hierarchy, not an expansion of Islamic space. To forget this origin story, while courting organisations that still carry the ideological DNA of those who opposed the liberation war, is to invite mutilation.

The Bangladesh Nationalist Party under Tarique Rahman is in a commanding parliamentary position, with Jamaat-e-Islami as the principal opposition. Rahman and his colleagues will attempt to neutralise the more radical Islamist currents, co-opting some, containing others, and presenting a face of pragmatic nationalism to investors and neighbours. The calculation is understandable. Yet the risk of excessive concession is real. Jamaat’s vote share and organisational discipline give it bargaining power. Put differently, Bangladesh is on a razor’s edge. Should the BNP yield too much ground in the name of coalition or street peace, Bangladesh could drift towards a soft Islamist settlement resembling the Muslim Brotherhood’s brief experiment in Egypt after 2011: electoral legitimacy followed by gradual institutional capture, polarisation and eventual institutional breakdown.

Egypt’s lesson travels poorly in some respects, but the core warning is transferable. When democratic forms produce governments unable or unwilling to restrain forces that reject the plural foundations of the state, external observers and domestic elites alike begin to conclude that democracy itself is a luxury the country cannot afford. The rising ill wind can still be redirected. The alternative is a familiar regional tragedy: a nation that won its independence against cultural contempt only to risk surrendering its hard-won identity to a different form of ideological domination.

(The writer is a senior journalist with expertise in defence. Views expressed are personal and do not necessarily reflect those of Firstpost.)

editorials.title: Haryanvi Is Part of Delhi’s History. So Why Is It Missing From Its Identity?
editorials.passage: “In the region of Hariyanau which has numerous villages, and whose inhabitants are ever happy, there is the large city called Dhilli, favoured by Indra, destroying hostile armies, a mass of wealth, boiling the blood of the enemy.” This is how Delhi is described in 1132 by the Agravala Digambara poet Shridhar in his hagiography of the 23rd Jain Tirthankara Parshvanath, as one of the big cities of the "Haryana region".In the beginning of the 20th century, the British official George Grierson, in his Linguistic Survey of India (1916), mentions a single language spoken in the districts of Delhi, Rohtak, Karnal, and Hisar, along with the South East corner of the state of Patiala (present day Narwana).The Hariana tract at this time referred to the tehsils of Hissar, Fatehabad, and Hansi, and the eastern part of Bhiwani tehsil. The language, what is today called 'Haryanvi', was known as Jatu in Delhi and Rohtak due to the bulk population of Jats speaking the language in Hariani, Deswali or Desari in the Hariana tract. It was also called Bangaru language in Karnal and Narwana. The survey returned 2.36 lakh speakers of the language from Delhi district. Geographically, Yamuna is the eastern boundary of the Haryanvi language, hence the Haryanvi-speaking region occupies the majority area west of Yamuna in Delhi. Haryanvi-speaking villages fall in the North, North West, West, South West and Southern parts of Delhi, along with many villages of what is now marked as ‘New Delhi’ in district classifications.The area is simply a continuation of the Sonipat-Rohtak-North Jhajjar linguistic belt, coexisting with the power concentration in areas like Shahjahanabad where Urdu was the native language. Similar situations existed in other power centres, be it Agra, where Urdu was spoken by the townsmen, while others spoke Braj Bhasha.The Politics of Language in India: A Battle of Identity and PowerGrierson for this very reason separates ‘Delhi City’ and ‘Delhi Mufassil’, where the city had a Urdu speaking population, while the Mufassil was of Haryanvi majority. Even many Muslims of Karnal city and some villages are reported to speak Urdu, while the majority spoke Haryanvi.The separation of Delhi District as a territory from this contiguous region as it acquired capital status, and the creation of the state of Haryana out of the other districts speaking the language began a saga of confusion. The language became singularly known as Haryanvi and became associated with the boundaries of the modern Haryana state. While Urdu, Hindi and Punjabi became official languages of Delhi, Haryanvi was nowhere to be found.The language today is in a peculiar situation in Delhi. There is a growing number of children who are not learning Haryanvi from their parents in their formative years, as parents fear the language is unsuitable to be taught. There was a proposal to create a Haryanvi Academy in a similar fashion to the Bhojpuri-Maithili and Garhwali-Kumaoni-Jaunsari academy, but no action was taken. People think that Haryanvi speakers have come from Haryana, and some are surprised to see the existence of Haryanvi speaking villages of Delhi. People confuse sites of the powers bygone with the totality of the erstwhile ‘Delhi District’.Without revitalisation and recognition, Haryanvi will be forgotten in Delhi. My mother, who studied till Class 10, and my father, who studied till Class 8, made sure I learnt English and spoke “proper” standard Hindi. Haryanvi, the language of my village Devli in South Delhi, was not encouraged. Hauz Khaz, Mehrauli, Burari, Dhaka: The Villages That Delhi Swallowed UpI remember once saying, “कि त जावेह?” (Ki ta javeh?) meaning “Where are you going?” to my cousin. My mother immediately scolded me, saying they were wasting their hard-earned money on my education. I do not see this as their fault. It was the mirror of a society that had taught them to see their own language as a burden. For Delhi’s villages, education meant distance from Haryanvi. Standard Hindi brings respectability while speaking English is the ultimate ladder to be seen as success.This article has inputs from Akshay Kumar, who runs the project Bhashakosh, documenting the regional languages, cultures, and geographies of India.(Puneet Singh Singhal is the Founder/Curator of Dilli Dehat Project, a community-led archive and storytelling initiative that documents the rural histories, cultures, and lived realities of Delhi’s villages. This is an opinion piece and the views expressed are the author's own. The Quint does not endorse or is responsible for them.)
